title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Blue-Green Deployment
summary: Blue-green deployment is a release strategy that runs two identical production environments — "blue" (the current live version) and "green" (the new version) — and switches traffic between them via a single router update, so…
objectives: What is blue-green deployment, and what problem does it solve that in-place upgrades do not?
How do you handle database schema changes in a blue-green deployment?
What is canary analysis, and how does it combine with blue-green?
What is the cost of blue-green, and how do teams with large fleets or tight margins adapt?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Blue-green deployment is a release strategy that runs two identical production environments — "blue" (the current live version) and "green" (the new version) — and switches traffic between them via a single router update, so deployment becomes an instant, reversible cutover rather than a slow, risky in-place upgrade.
Every system must change, and every change carries risk — a new version may have a bug, a performance regression, or an unexpected interaction with the production data. The traditional release pattern is "in-place upgrade": stop the old version, install the new version, restart, and hope nothing breaks. If something breaks, you are down until you reverse the upgrade, and reverse upgrades are notoriously unreliable (databases rarely downgrade cleanly). Blue-green deployment eliminates this class of risk by maintaining two complete, parallel environments. The "blue" environment is the currently live one serving all production traffic. The "green" environment is a fresh deployment of the new version, running on identical infrastructure but receiving zero traffic. When green is verified (smoke tests, canary checks, manual validation), a single router update — flipping the load balancer's target group or DNS record — moves all traffic from blue to green in seconds. If green misbehaves, the same router update flipped back restores blue instantly. Amazon popularized this pattern in the early 2010s; Netflix adopted it as "red/black deployment" via their Spinnaker platform, and it is now the default release strategy at every mature engineering organization.

The first concept is the two environments. Blue and green must be functionally identical — same instance types, same database, same network configuration, same autoscaling policies — so that the cutover does not introduce performance or behavioral surprises. The only difference is the software version. This is harder than it sounds: if blue uses an older schema and green expects a newer schema, the database must be migrated before the cutover, and the migration must be backward-compatible (green must work against the new schema, blue must also work against the new schema during the transition window). The standard pattern is "expand-and-contract" schema migrations: first deploy a version that supports both old and new schema (the "expand" step), then migrate the database, then deploy a version that uses only the new schema (the "contract" step). Without this discipline, green will crash on the new schema while blue is still expecting the old, and the cutover becomes a one-way door.

The second concept is the router as the single source of truth. The router — typically a load balancer (AWS ALB, NGINX, HAProxy) or a DNS record (Route 53 weighted policy) — is the only thing that decides which environment receives traffic. In the simplest pattern, the router points 100% at blue; after verification, it points 100% at green; on rollback, it points 100% back at blue. The cutover is one configuration change, taking seconds, and is fully reversible. A more sophisticated pattern is canary within blue-green: after deploying green, shift 1% of traffic to it, watch error rates and latency for 10 minutes, shift to 5%, watch, shift to 25%, watch, shift to 100%. This combines blue-green's reversibility with canary's gradual exposure, catching bugs that only manifest under production load. Netflix's Spinnaker platform automates this entire flow: deploy to green, run automated canary analysis comparing green's metrics to blue's, and either promote to 100% or roll back automatically based on statistical significance.

The third concept is the database challenge. Stateless applications are trivial to blue-green — the new version is just code, and the cutover is purely a router change. Stateful applications with a shared database are harder: the database cannot be duplicated (it would diverge during the cutover), so blue and green must share one database. This means the new version's code must work against the current schema (forward-compatible) and the old version's code must work against any new schema (backward-compatible) — both during the transition window. The expand-and-contract pattern handles this: deploy green with code that supports both old and new schema, migrate the database, cut over to green, then deploy a future version that drops the old schema. For breaking schema changes that cannot be made backward-compatible, the pattern is "shadow writes" — green writes to a new table while blue continues to write to the old, and a backfill job copies data between them; cutover happens only when both tables are in sync. The cost is significant engineering complexity; the benefit is zero-downtime, reversible releases even for stateful services.

The fourth concept is the cost. Blue-green requires roughly 2× the production infrastructure during the cutover window — you are running both environments simultaneously. If your production fleet is 100 instances, blue-green means 100 blue plus 100 green during the release. For most teams this is acceptable because the cutover window is short (minutes to hours), and the cost is amortized over the release cadence (weekly releases mean 2× cost for a few hours per week, perhaps 5% additional monthly cost). For teams with very large fleets or very tight margins, the compromise is "rolling blue-green" — keep a small green environment (10% of production capacity) for canary, then either scale it up to 100% for the cutover or accept a rolling in-place upgrade for the rest. Netflix, Amazon, and Google absorb the full 2× cost because they release hundreds of times per day and the operational safety is worth it; smaller teams often use blue-green only for high-risk releases (database migrations, major version upgrades) and rolling deploys for routine releases.

The fifth concept is automated canary analysis. The bottleneck in blue-green is human judgment — an engineer must look at green's metrics (error rate, latency, CPU, custom business metrics) and decide whether to promote or roll back. This is slow (a careful engineer takes 20–60 minutes per release) and error-prone (subtle regressions are easy to miss in a wall of dashboards). Automated canary analysis, pioneered by Netflix's Kayenta, compares green's metrics to blue's using statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U for distribution shifts, t-tests for mean changes) and produces a score: if green is statistically indistinguishable from blue, promote; if green is worse on any key metric, roll back. The system runs in minutes, catches subtle regressions humans would miss, and scales to hundreds of releases per day. Amazon'sDeployinator, Google's progressive rollout, and Microsoft's Safe Deployment System all use similar techniques. The trade-off is that automated analysis requires high-quality metrics and a baseline of historical variance to know what "statistically indistinguishable" means; for new services with sparse metrics, human judgment is still needed.

The sixth concept is the operational discipline. Blue-green is not just a deployment technique — it is a cultural commitment to "every release is reversible" and "no release is irreversible." This requires: infrastructure as code (both environments are deployed identically via Terraform/CloudFormation), automated tests that run on green before cutover, monitoring that distinguishes blue's metrics from green's, a rollback procedure that is rehearsed (not just documented), and a release calendar that respects the operational cost (no releases on Friday afternoon if the team wants a quiet weekend). Netflix's red/black deploys on Spinnaker are fully automated: a developer pushes code, Spinnaker deploys to green, runs canary analysis, and either promotes or rolls back — the developer does not touch production. The trade-off summary: blue-green delivers zero-downtime, reversible releases at the cost of 2× infrastructure during cutover, significant engineering investment in tooling and schema-migration discipline, and a cultural commitment to operational excellence. For teams that release frequently or where downtime is costly, the investment pays back rapidly; for teams that release rarely and have generous maintenance windows, simpler strategies (rolling deploys, in-place upgrades) may be sufficient.

compare green vs blue metrics] Analyze -->|pass| Promote[Router 100% -> green] Analyze -->|fail| Rollback[Router stays 100% blue] Promote --> Drain[Drain blue, keep warm for rollback] Drain --> Cleanup[Terminate blue after 24h] end Promote -.->|router update| Router Rollback -.->|router stays| Router ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` before cutover: after cutover: =============== ============= users users | | v v +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ | Router | 100% ---> | BLUE v1.5| | Router | 100% ---> | GREEN v1.6| | (ALB/DNS)| | live | | (ALB/DNS)| | live | +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ | | +-- 0% ---> +----------+ +-- 0% ---> +----------+ | GREEN v1.6| | BLUE v1.5 | | staged | | warm standby | +----------+ +----------+ cutover = single router update, ~5 seconds, fully reversible canary within blue-green (gradual exposure): T=0 deploy green, smoke test 0% traffic T=5m shift 1% to green, watch metrics 1% traffic T=15m shift 5% to green, watch 5% traffic T=25m shift 25% to green, watch 25% traffic T=35m shift 100% to green 100% traffic (blue drained) T=35m keep blue warm for 1h rollback window, then terminate ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Build the new version (v1.6) and deploy it to the green environment, which is provisioned identically to blue but receives zero traffic; run smoke tests against green's endpoints to verify basic functionality. 2. Shift a small percentage of traffic (1%) to green, run automated canary analysis comparing green's metrics to blue's, and progressively increase to 5%, 25%, 100% as each stage passes; if any stage fails, the router automatically returns to 100% blue. 3. After cutover, keep blue warm for a rollback window (typically 1–24 hours); if no rollback is needed, drain and terminate blue, completing the release.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Blue-green deployment orchestrator.
- Snapshot of an environment's key metrics for canary analysis.
- State machine for a blue-green deployment.
- Run smoke tests against green before any traffic shift.
- Canary stages: percent of traffic to green at each step.
- Hard thresholds: green must meet absolute SLOs.
- Relative regression: green must not be much worse than blue.
- Blue is the current live version with healthy production metrics.

**Defines:** `Metrics`, `Environment`, `Thresholds`, `BlueGreenOrchestrator`

```python
"""
Blue-green deployment orchestrator.

Demonstrates the logic that Spinnaker / Argo Rollouts / AWS CodeDeploy
perform: deploy to green, run health gates, gradually shift traffic,
auto-rollback on regression.

This is the decision engine — it does not call real cloud APIs but
models the state machine and the canary analysis that production
blue-green systems use.
"""
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List

@dataclass
class Metrics:
    """Snapshot of an environment's key metrics for canary analysis."""
    error_rate: float       # 0.0 - 1.0
    p99_latency_ms: float
    cpu_pct: float
    rps: float              # requests per second

@dataclass
class Environment:
    name: str               # 'blue' or 'green'
    version: str
    live: bool = False      # receiving production traffic?
    healthy: bool = True
    metrics: Metrics = field(default_factory=lambda: Metrics(0, 0, 0, 0))

@dataclass
class Thresholds:
    max_error_rate: float = 0.01         # 1%
    max_p99_latency_ms: float = 500.0
    max_latency_regression_pct: float = 20.0  # green can be 20% slower than blue

class BlueGreenOrchestrator:
    """State machine for a blue-green deployment."""

    # Canary stages: percent of traffic to green at each step.
    STAGES = [0, 1, 5, 25, 100]

    def __init__(self, blue: Environment, green: Environment,
                 thresholds: Thresholds = Thresholds()):
        self.blue = blue
        self.green = green
        self.thresholds = thresholds
        self.traffic_pct_green = 0   # 0 = all blue, 100 = all green
        self.history: List[Dict] = []

    def _record(self, stage: str, msg: str) -> None:
        self.history.append({"stage": stage, "msg": msg,
                             "green_pct": self.traffic_pct_green,
                             "ts": time.time()})
        print(f"  [{stage:>10}] green={self.traffic_pct_green:>3}%  {msg}")

    def smoke_test(self, probe: Callable[[Environment], bool]) -> bool:
        """Run smoke tests against green before any traffic shift."""
        self._record("smoke", "running smoke tests on green (0% traffic)")
        ok = probe(self.green)
        if not ok:
            self._record("smoke", "FAIL - smoke tests failed, abort")
            return False
        self._record("smoke", "PASS - green basic checks ok")
        return True

    def canary_analyze(self) -> bool:
        """Compare green's metrics to blue's; return True if green is acceptable."""
        b, g = self.blue.metrics, self.green.metrics
        # Hard thresholds: green must meet absolute SLOs.
        if g.error_rate > self.thresholds.max_error_rate:
            self._record("analyze", f"FAIL error_rate {g.error_rate:.3f} > "
                          f"{self.thresholds.max_error_rate}")
            return False
        if g.p99_latency_ms > self.thresholds.max_p99_latency_ms:
            self._record("analyze", f"FAIL p99 {g.p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms > "
                          f"{self.thresholds.max_p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms")
            return False
        # Relative regression: green must not be much worse than blue.
        if b.p99_latency_ms > 0:
            regression = ((g.p99_latency_ms - b.p99_latency_ms)
                          / b.p99_latency_ms * 100)
            if regression > self.thresholds.max_latency_regression_pct:
                self._record("analyze", f"FAIL latency regression "
                              f"{regression:.1f}% > "
                              f"{self.thresholds.max_latency_regression_pct}%")
                return False
        self._record("analyze",
                      f"PASS  green err={g.error_rate:.3f} "
                      f"p99={g.p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms "
                      f"(blue err={b.error_rate:.3f} "
                      f"p99={b.p99_latency_ms:.0f}ms)")
        return True

    def shift_traffic(self, target_pct: int) -> None:
        """Move traffic to green (simulated router update)."""
        self.traffic_pct_green = target_pct
        if target_pct == 100:
            self.green.live = True
            self.blue.live = False
            self._record("promote", "100% traffic on green, blue drained")
        elif target_pct == 0:
            self.green.live = False
            self.blue.live = True
            self._record("rollback", "0% traffic on green, blue restored")
        else:
            self._record("canary", f"{target_pct}% canary on green")

    def deploy(self, probe: Callable[[Environment], bool]) -> bool:
        """Full blue-green deployment with canary stages."""
        print(f"== deploying {self.green.version} to green ==")
        if not self.smoke_test(probe):
            return False
        for stage in self.STAGES[1:]:    # skip 0
            self.shift_traffic(stage)
            if not self.canary_analyze():
                self.shift_traffic(0)    # rollback
                print("== deployment FAILED, rolled back to blue ==")
                return False
        print("== deployment SUCCEEDED, green is live ==")
        return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Blue is the current live version with healthy production metrics.
    blue = Environment("blue", "v1.5", live=True,
                       metrics=Metrics(error_rate=0.005,
                                       p99_latency_ms=200,
                                       cpu_pct=45, rps=1000))
    # Green is the new version; metrics represent what canary analysis sees.
    green = Environment("green", "v1.6", live=False,
                        metrics=Metrics(error_rate=0.004,
                                        p99_latency_ms=210,
                                        cpu_pct=47, rps=1000))

    def smoke(env: Environment) -> bool:
        # In production this would hit /health, /smoke, etc.
        return env.version == "v1.6"

    orch = BlueGreenOrchestrator(blue, green)
    success = orch.deploy(smoke)

    print("\n== history ==")
    for h in orch.history:
        print(f"  {h['stage']:>10}  green={h['green_pct']:>3}%  {h['msg']}")
    print(f"\nresult: {'SUCCESS' if success else 'ROLLED BACK'}")
    print(f"blue live={blue.live}, green live={green.live}")
```
